traveler: Juan Manuel José Domingo Ortiz de Rozas y López de Osornio (Juan Manuel de Rosas)
title: The Restorer of the Laws: the Estancia, the Suma del Poder Público, and the Farm at Swaythling
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Buenos Aires, birth on the calle Santa Lucía
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In his mother's house on the calle Santa Lucía, between Florida and San Martín, Agustina López de Osornio bears a son to León Ortiz de Rosas, and he is christened Juan Manuel José Domingo. The family holds land south of the city and the boy is raised to it before he is raised to anything else. At eight he is enrolled in the private school of Francisco Javier Argerich, one of the few the viceregal capital keeps; he learns letters there and little else that will matter later. The surname he will shorten to Rosas is at this date still Ortiz de Rozas.
suggested_refs: The block of the calle Santa Lucía, today Sarmiento, between Florida and San Martín, site of the maternal house

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the British invasions
stops.date_confidence: year only: the pool dates the ammunition detail to 1806, the year of the Reconquista, and his part in the defense of the city to 1807; neither is given a day, so the entry defaults to 1 January
stops.campa: British troops take Buenos Aires and the city takes it back without waiting for Spain. Rosas is thirteen. He carries ammunition through the streets during the Reconquista, and when the second invasion comes the following year he is among the armed townsmen on the rooftops and behind the barricades. Twice in two summers, townsmen and militia raised out of the countryside beat a European army in the streets with no help from the crown. The viceroyalty has three years left to run, and the men who did the beating are still riding forty years later.
suggested_refs: The Reconquista of 1806 and the Defensa of 1807, the two actions in which Rosas first bore arms

stops.name: Rincón de López, the estancias of his mother
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Spanish biography places him on the López de Osornio estancias south of the Salado from roughly 1807 to 1815 without giving a date or a coordinate; the pin is approximate and the year is inferred
stops.campa: He leaves the city for the estancias his mother holds south of the río Salado, frontier country where the herds run unfenced and the nearest authority is a day's ride. He learns to ride, to brand, to slaughter, to give orders to peons and to take none. The gauchos accept him because he does everything they do, longer and better than they do it. This is the whole of his schooling after Argerich. The militia he raises later, and the government he runs later still, are run on the discipline of a cattle station.
suggested_refs: The López de Osornio estancias south of the río Salado, the schooling that replaced Argerich's

stops.name: Buenos Aires, marriage to Encarnación Ezcurra
stops.date_confidence: year only: both Wikipedias give 1813 for the marriage without a day; the children's dates that follow are day-precise in the Spanish biography
stops.campa: He marries Encarnación Ezcurra y Arguibel, of a porteño family with more name than money, and she proves the sharper politician of the two. Their son Juan Bautista is born on 30 July 1814; their daughter Manuela, who will be called Manuelita and will keep her father's house for the rest of his life, on 24 May 1817. Encarnación will build the street power of the federal party in the city while her husband holds the countryside, and the popular league that becomes the mazorca answers to her before it answers to him.
suggested_refs: The Ezcurra family papers, and Encarnación's correspondence with her husband during the 1833 campaign

stops.name: Los Cerrillos, the estancia and the Colorados del Monte
stops.date_confidence: year only for the purchase; the enlistment of the militia as the Fifth Regiment is dated 1820 by the English article and is carried in the pool as a reconstruction, while the suppression of Pagola's mutiny is attested to 1 October 1820
stops.campa: He buys the estancia Los Cerrillos at San Miguel del Monte and turns it into a barracks. Out of his own peons and the frontier riders he raises a cavalry militia dressed in red, known as the Colorados del Monte, which the province enrolls as the Fifth Regiment of Militia. In October 1820, with the mutineer Manuel Pagola holding part of the city and the government of Buenos Aires reduced to a few streets, the Colorados ride in and put the rebellion down. The estanciero is now the man the state calls when it cannot hold its own capital.
suggested_refs: The casco of Los Cerrillos at San Miguel del Monte, quarters of the Colorados del Monte

stops.name: Estancia del Pino, La Matanza
stops.date_confidence: year only: the Spanish biography dates the acquisition to 1821 and the tenure to 1821-1824; the coordinate is approximate to the partido of La Matanza, the casco is not located in the source
stops.campa: He takes over the old estancia of the viceroy Joaquín del Pino in La Matanza and renames it San Martín, adding it to Los Cerrillos, to Camarones beyond the Salado, and to a spread of pasture no one in the province can match. Twelve years later a young English naturalist riding through his camp will write down what the country says about the size of it. The cattle pay the militia, feed the city and buy the loyalty of men who own nothing, and their hides are the only export the port of Buenos Aires has to sell to anyone.
stops.quote: He is said to be the owner of seventy-four square leagues of land, and to have about three hundred thousand head of cattle.
stops.quote_source: Charles Darwin, Voyage of the Beagle, Chapter 4, reporting contemporary estimates in 1833
suggested_refs: The estancia del Pino in La Matanza, renamed San Martín, and the surviving Rosas estancia inventories
sources: Charles Darwin, Voyage of the Beagle, ch. 4

stops.name: Buenos Aires, comandante general de milicias
stops.date_confidence: year only: the Spanish biography dates the appointment to 1827 without a day
stops.campa: Governor Manuel Dorrego, a federal, names him comandante general de milicias, placing the armed countryside of Buenos Aires province formally in the hands of the man who already commands it in fact. The unitarios in the city read the appointment correctly and hate it. Rosas is thirty-four. He owns leagues of pasture and keeps a regiment he raised and pays out of his own pocket, and he now carries a commission from the governor over both. From this year forward no office in the province can be filled against his objection.
suggested_refs: Dorrego's decree of 1827 creating the general command of militias

stops.name: Navarro, Dorrego defeated and shot
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool's own geography lens originally put Rosas on the field here, which the Spanish article on the battle contradicts
stops.campa: Lavalle comes back from the Brazilian war, overthrows Dorrego and pursues him into the campaña. Dorrego means to join Rosas and the militias of the north; he gives up the plan and offers battle alone at Navarro, where six hundred cuirassiers ride down two thousand gauchos in a few minutes. He is taken and shot shortly after, on Lavalle's order, without trial. The federal party has its martyr. Rosas, who was not on the field, is the only federal chief left standing with an army, and the war that follows will be fought over an execution rather than over a constitution.
suggested_refs: The field of Navarro and the site of Dorrego's execution, 13 December 1828

stops.name: Puente de Márquez, the federal victory
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The federal forces of Rosas and Estanislao López of Santa Fe meet Lavalle at Puente de Márquez, west of the city, and beat him. The war that began with Dorrego's execution is decided out in the countryside, by mounted men off the estancias against a professional officer corps that has nowhere left to recruit. Lavalle is left holding a city and nothing around it. Within two months he will be riding out to negotiate with the man whose party he had tried to finish.
suggested_refs: The crossing at Puente de Márquez on the río Reconquista

stops.name: La Caledonia, Cañuelas: the pact with Lavalle
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the coordinate is approximate to the partido of Cañuelas, the estancia is named in the source but not located
stops.campa: At a farm near the Cañuelas post, held by an Englishman named Miller, Lavalle and Rosas sign the pact that closes the civil war of 1828 and 1829. They agree on a joint list for the legislature and on a provisional governor. The arrangement collapses within weeks and is superseded by a second agreement, but the meeting itself is the settlement: the defeated unitario general has come out to the campaña to treat with the estanciero, and the treating is done at a kitchen table on a cattle station rather than in the Fuerte.
suggested_refs: The Pacto de Cañuelas, 24 June 1829, and the Pacto de Barracas that superseded it

stops.name: Buenos Aires, proclaimed Restaurador de las Leyes
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Sala de Representantes elects him governor and captain general of the province, confers on him the title Restaurador de las Leyes, restorer of the laws, and votes him facultades extraordinarias, the emergency powers that suspend the ordinary limits of the office. He is thirty-six. The laws he is to restore are not written down anywhere, and the extraordinary faculties are granted for a term that keeps being renewed. The federal party has its government, and the countryside and the capital answer for the first time to one head.
stops.quote: the restorer of the laws and institutions of the Province of Buenos Ayres
stops.quote_source: Domingo Faustino Sarmiento, Civilization and Barbarism, trans. Mrs. Horace Mann, Preface
suggested_refs: The act of the Sala de Representantes of 8 December 1829 conferring the title and the facultades extraordinarias
sources: Sarmiento, Civilization and Barbarism, trans. Mann

stops.name: Santa Fe, the Pacto Federal signed without him
stops.date_confidence: attested for the signing; the coordinate for the city of Santa Fe is supplied from general geography, no lens in the pool carries one
stops.campa: In Santa Fe, José María Roxas y Patrón signs for Buenos Aires, Domingo Cullen for Santa Fe and Diego Miranda for Entre Ríos: a league of the three river provinces recognizing each other's autonomy and binding themselves against the unitario army of the interior. Rosas is not there. He governs the signature by written instruction from Buenos Aires, and he has no interest in the national constitution the pact promises for a later day. Corrientes accedes in August. The confederation that will bear his name is founded on a document he did not sign.
suggested_refs: The text of the Pacto Federal of 4 January 1831 and Rosas's instructions to Roxas y Patrón

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the first term ends
stops.date_confidence: contested: the Spanish biography gives 17 December 1832, the English article and the Spanish list of governors both give 5 December 1832, and the pool's chronology lens carried 18 December; the conflict is left open and the Spanish biography's date is used
stops.campa: He gives up the governorship at the end of his three-year term and refuses to stand again on terms he considers inadequate. Juan Ramón Balcarce succeeds him. He keeps the militias, the estancias, the party in the streets that his wife runs, and the title of Restaurador. What he gives up is the desk. The men who take the office will spend the next twenty-eight months finding out that it was the smaller half of the power, and the countryside will spend them waiting for him to come back on conditions of his own choosing.
suggested_refs: The Balcarce, Viamonte and Maza interim governments, 1832-1835
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Anexo:Gobernadores de la provincia de Buenos Aires'

stops.name: Los Cerrillos, departure for the Campaña al Desierto
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He rides out of Los Cerrillos at the head of a column of the Campaña al Desierto, the campaign to clear the southern frontier of the peoples of the pampa and open their grazing to the estancias. Three columns move south. He pays some tribes to kill the members of others, gives rations and drink and treaties to those who submit, and hunts the rest. The war is fought across exactly the country he has spent his life learning, and it adds to the province more land than the province was then using.
suggested_refs: The three columns of the 1833 Campaña al Desierto and their routes south of the Salado

stops.name: Río Colorado, the camp where Darwin comes
stops.date_confidence: year only, and the coordinate is contested: the geography lens gave a point that does not match its own Pedro Luro referent, the quotes lens gives another sixty leagues west; the pin follows the correction toward Pedro Luro on the river
stops.campa: The column camps on the río Colorado, the southern limit of the advance. Into the camp rides Charles Darwin, twenty-four years old, off the Beagle and crossing the pampa overland to Buenos Aires; he needs a passport through the lines and Rosas gives him one. Darwin watches the general among his men and writes him down: a perfect horseman, grave in conversation, dressed and speaking as the gauchos do, holding an unbounded power in consequence. He also records what the camp says about the standing order to kill stragglers.
stops.quote: He is a man of an extraordinary character, and has a most predominant influence in the country, which it seems probable he will use to its prosperity and advancement.
stops.quote_source: Charles Darwin, Voyage of the Beagle, Chapter 4, on meeting Rosas at the Rio Colorado camp, 1833
suggested_refs: Darwin's Beagle diary and the passport issued to him by Rosas at the Colorado
sources: Charles Darwin, Voyage of the Beagle, chs. 4 and 5

stops.name: Napostá, the campaign ends
stops.date_confidence: contested: the Spanish biography states verbatim that the campaign ended on 25 May 1834, and the pool's geography lens carried 25 May 1833 for the same event; 1834 is used and the pairing of Napostá with the exact day is an inference, since the source mentions the farewell address without dating it
stops.campa: At Napostá, near Bahía Blanca, he closes the campaign and addresses the troops before turning north. The reckoning given out is thousands of Indians killed or taken and hundreds of captives recovered, and the country south of the Salado is open. He returns to Buenos Aires and refuses the honors the legislature votes him: the sword, the money, the governorship again. Each refusal raises the price of the next offer. The frontier line he fixes here holds until Julio Argentino Roca carries it to the Río Negro forty-five years later.
suggested_refs: The arroyo Napostá near Bahía Blanca, and Rosas's farewell address to the columns

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the suma del poder público
stops.date_confidence: attested; two distinct acts are often conflated, the grant of the suma del poder público on 7 March 1835 and the formal naming as governor by the Sala on 13 April 1835 after the plebiscite, and the English article dates the second term from 7 March
stops.campa: Facundo Quiroga is shot with his escort at Barranca Yaco in Córdoba on 16 February, and the confederation loses the one caudillo whose weight matched his own. Three weeks later the legislature votes Rosas the suma del poder público, the whole public power, without division and without appeal. He demands that the people confirm it: the plebiscite of 28 March returns nine thousand seven hundred and thirteen votes in favor and seven against. On 13 April the Sala names him governor. He holds the office for seventeen years.
suggested_refs: The law of 7 March 1835 granting the suma del poder público, and the parish registers of the March plebiscite

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the pension of Doña Remedios Rosas
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: By decree of the governor, María Remedios del Valle is placed on the army's inactive roster as sargento mayor. She had carried water and cartridges through the field hospitals of the northern army twenty years before, had been flogged by the royalists, and had been begging in the streets of Buenos Aires ever since the war ended. In gratitude she takes the governor's surname and signs herself Doña Remedios Rosas until her death in the city in 1847. The decree is signed in the first weeks of the suma del poder público.
suggested_refs: The decree of 16 April 1835 restoring María Remedios del Valle to the army rolls

stops.name: Río de la Plata, the French blockade
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Spanish article on the blockade, which gives Wednesday 28 March 1838; the pool's chronology lens carried 28 February 1839 for the same event, wrong by nearly a year, and the two lenses contradicted each other
stops.campa: France demands consular privilege and exemption from military service for its citizens, Rosas refuses, and a French squadron closes the port of Buenos Aires. The blockade holds for two and a half years, strangling the customs revenue that is the province's only income, and it does not move him. In the same year he sends Carlos María de Alvear to Washington as minister plenipotentiary, where Alvear spends fourteen years explaining the government of Rosas to five successive presidents of the United States. France lifts the blockade in October 1840.
suggested_refs: The French blockade of the Río de la Plata, 28 March 1838 to 29 October 1840
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Bloqueo francés del Río de la Plata'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the death of Encarnación Ezcurra
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Spanish article on Encarnación Ezcurra; the pool's chronology lens gave only October 1838, and its geography lens wrongly placed the death at the Palermo caserón, which did not yet exist
stops.campa: Encarnación Ezcurra dies at forty-three. The cortege goes from the Fuerte to the convent of San Francisco with the government and the garrison behind it, and she is laid in the family vault at the Recoleta. She had built the popular federalism of the city out of nothing while her husband was in the campaña: the network of informers, the women of the parishes, the armed league that becomes the mazorca. Rosas does not marry again. He takes María Eugenia Castro into the house, and nobody takes over what his wife had been doing.
suggested_refs: The Ortiz de Rozas vault at the Recoleta, where Encarnación is buried in 1838

stops.name: Palermo, the caserón of San Benito
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the Spanish article on the caserón puts the start of construction around 1838, after Encarnación's death, continuing into the mid-1840s; no completion date is given and the year here is defaulted to 1 January
stops.campa: On the low ground of Palermo, east of the city and swampy enough that carriages sink in it, he begins building the caserón of San Benito: a great low quadrangle of galleries and patios, guarded, raised on earth hauled by the cartload, with an orange grove and a lake. Government moves out there with him. Ministers, ambassadors and petitioners make the ride out of Buenos Aires to a house standing in a marsh. He governs from it for fourteen years, and Manuelita receives in it on his behalf on almost every evening of them.
suggested_refs: The Caserón de Rosas at San Benito de Palermo, at the eastern corner of today's Avenida General Sarmiento and Avenida del Libertador

stops.name: Pago Largo, Corrientes broken
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool's geography lens placed the field roughly two hundred kilometres out of position, in central Corrientes, and the pin here follows the correction toward Curuzú Cuatiá
stops.campa: Corrientes rises against the confederation under Genaro Berón de Astrada, and the federal army of Entre Ríos under Pascual Echagüe destroys it at Pago Largo. Berón de Astrada is brought down with boleadoras and lanced on the field. The littoral is quiet again for some years. In the north the unitario general Juan Lavalle, who had Dorrego shot eleven years before, campaigns against the government through the years of the French blockade; he is dead in Jujuy by October 1841, and after him no unitario army takes the field for a decade.
suggested_refs: The field of Pago Largo near Curuzú Cuatiá, Corrientes

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the Maza conspiracy
stops.date_confidence: month only: the pool gives June 1839 without a day, so the entry defaults to the first
stops.campa: A conspiracy of the city's unitarios is uncovered in June. Manuel Vicente Maza, president of the Sala de Representantes and an old servant of the government, is implicated; he is killed in the Sala itself, and those taken with him are shot. From this month the mazorca works in the open: house searches, the red ribbon required on every hat and every lapel, the whitewashing of anything painted in the sky blue of the unitarios. Terror in Buenos Aires becomes an instrument of administration rather than an excess of one.
stops.quote: Death to the dirty savages, Unitarios
stops.quote_source: Domingo Faustino Sarmiento, Civilization and Barbarism, trans. Mrs. Horace Mann, Chapter 8, giving the device Rosas ordered stamped on the mandatory federal ribbon
suggested_refs: Surviving federal ribbons and hat devices bearing the mueran los salvajes unitarios formula
sources: Sarmiento, Civilization and Barbarism, trans. Mann

stops.name: Cerrito de la Victoria, the siege of Montevideo
stops.date_confidence: year only for the opening of the siege, which the pool dates 1843-1851 without a day; the Spanish article consulted documents the hill but does not narrate the siege
stops.campa: Manuel Oribe, ally of Rosas and deposed president of Uruguay, lays siege to Montevideo from the hill of the Cerrito and does not leave for nine years. Inside the walls are the Argentine exiles who write against Rosas, the French and Italian legions, Garibaldi. Sarmiento comes through and finds his own Facundo already being read there, the book he had written in Chile for the express purpose of wrecking a diplomatic mission of the Buenos Aires government. They call it the Sitio Grande, and it settles nothing.
suggested_refs: The Cerrito de la Victoria, Oribe's headquarters through the Sitio Grande of Montevideo

stops.name: India Muerta, Rivera broken
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Spanish article on the battle, though the pool carried this as a reconstruction with an approximate coordinate; the pin remains approximate to the arroyo India Muerta in northern Rocha
stops.campa: On the arroyo India Muerta in the north of Rocha, Justo José de Urquiza brings four thousand Entre Ríos federals and two thousand Uruguayan blancos against Fructuoso Rivera and destroys him. Rivera runs for Brazil with thousands of followers behind him. It is the high point of the confederation's war in the Banda Oriental and the making of the general who wins it. Seven years from this field, Urquiza will cross the Paraná with an army raised against Rosas and finish him in a single morning.
suggested_refs: The arroyo India Muerta, Rocha Department, Uruguay, field of 27 March 1845

stops.name: Río de la Plata, the Anglo-French blockade
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Britain and France close the port again, this time to force the opening of the Paraná and the Uruguay to their own merchant traffic. Rosas answers that the rivers are interior waters of the confederation and that no foreign flag passes them without permission. From Grand Bourg near Paris, José de San Martín, who has not set foot in the country for a quarter of a century, offers his services to the government against the invaders; in his testament of the year before he leaves his sabre of the Andes to Rosas for the firmness with which he sustained the honor of the republic.
suggested_refs: San Martín's Paris testament of 1844 and the clause bequeathing the sabre of the Andes to Rosas

stops.name: Vuelta de Obligado, the chains across the Paraná
stops.date_confidence: attested; the coordinate follows the Spanish article on the battle, and both the geography and afterlife lenses of the pool carried different and wrong points for the same site
stops.campa: Where the Paraná narrows at Obligado, Lucio Mansilla stretches boats across the river on chains and lays four batteries along the bank under Alzogaray, Eduardo Brown, Palacios and Thorne. The Anglo-French squadron comes up on the morning of 20 November, fights the day out, cuts the chains and forces the passage. The batteries are taken and the river is open. The convoy that goes upstream finds nobody willing to trade with it, and the cost of the operation persuades London and Paris to concede what their guns had just denied.
suggested_refs: The monument at the Vuelta de Obligado, San Pedro partido, and the surviving chain links
sources: es.wikipedia.org, 'Batalla de la Vuelta de Obligado'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the two treaties
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Arana-Southern treaty of 15 July 1847; the Arana-Lepredour treaty with France is dated 12 June 1848 and the last of the blockade is lifted in 1850, all three carried in one stop
stops.campa: Felipe Arana signs with Britain in July 1847 and with France eleven months later: the Arana-Southern and Arana-Lepredour conventions end the hostilities and lift, in turn, each power's share of the blockade. The last of it is gone by 1850. Rosas has outlasted the two strongest navies in the world by refusing for five years to concede a point neither government was willing to fight a full war over, and the rivers of the interior remain, in law and in practice, internal waters of the confederation.
suggested_refs: The Arana-Southern convention of 1847 and the Arana-Lepredour convention of 1848

stops.name: Santos Lugares, Camila O'Gorman shot
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the coordinate is approximate to the locality of Santos Lugares in San Andrés, supplied from the named place because no lens in the pool carries a point for it
stops.campa: Camila O'Gorman, of one of the best families in the city, had run off with Ladislao Gutiérrez, a priest. They are taken and held at the prison camp of Santos Lugares outside Buenos Aires, and Rosas orders the two of them shot by firing squad. There is no trial and no sentence; the historian John Lynch records that the order is personal and that it is carried out without any proceeding at all. Of all the killings of the seventeen years this is the one the city does not absorb, and the only one of them it still remembers by name.
suggested_refs: The prison camp of Santos Lugares in San Andrés, and John Lynch's account of the execution

stops.name: Buenos Aires, war declared on Brazil
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He declares war on the Empire of Brazil. Brazil, Uruguay and the province of Entre Ríos are already in league against him, and the coalition is commanded by Urquiza, who had won India Muerta for the confederation six years before. Rosas has quarreled with the only federal army outside Buenos Aires and gone to war with a monarchy in the same season. The Ejército Grande crosses the Paraná at Diamante with twenty-four thousand men, and Sarmiento is with it as lieutenant colonel, in charge of the press wagon and the bulletins.
suggested_refs: The crossing of the Paraná at Diamante and Sarmiento's field press with the Ejército Grande

stops.name: Caseros, the Ejército Grande
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the coordinate is the atlas pin already carried for Caseros in the Sarmiento journey, and it disagrees by some twenty kilometres with the Spanish article's siting of the battle at El Palomar, a conflict left open
stops.campa: The Ejército Grande comes on at Caseros: Entre Ríos and Corrientes cavalry, Brazilian infantry and artillery, Uruguayan blancos turned against him, twenty-four thousand men against a slightly smaller army that has not fought a European-style battle in twenty years. It lasts six hours. The line goes, and Rosas rides off the field. Seventeen years of the suma del poder público end in a single morning on a plain west of the city, and the man who ends them is the general who had served the confederation best.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Caseros at El Palomar and the Ejército Grande's order of battle

stops.name: Hueco de los Sauces, the resignation
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He comes into the city and stops at the Hueco de los Sauces, open ground on the southern edge of Buenos Aires where the carters water their horses. There he writes out his resignation as governor and captain general of the province, dates it the third of February, and has it carried to the legislature that had renewed his powers every year since 1835. The paper is a few lines long. Then he goes to the house of the British consul, and by nightfall the government he held for seventeen years is a question for other men.
stops.quote: Creo haber llenado mi deber con mis conciudadanos.
stops.quote_source: Rosas's letter of resignation written at the Hueco de los Sauces, 3 February 1852, as given in es.wikipedia.org, 'Batalla de Caseros'
suggested_refs: The Hueco de los Sauces, today Plaza Garay, where the resignation was written

stops.name: Puerto de Buenos Aires, aboard the Centaur
stops.date_confidence: month only: the pool gives February 1852 for the embarkation without a day, so the entry defaults to the first, though the departure follows the 3 February battle
stops.campa: Robert Gore, the British consul, takes him in within hours of the defeat and arranges the departure under a foreign flag. He goes aboard the British warship Centaur in the roads off Buenos Aires with Manuelita and a few of the household, and the ship stands out into the estuary. He is fifty-eight. Behind him the caserón at Palermo is being stripped, his herds are being counted by the victors, and the legislature that voted him the whole public power is preparing to vote his property to the treasury.
suggested_refs: Robert Gore's consular dispatches on sheltering Rosas and arranging his passage

stops.name: Plymouth, the salute of twenty-one guns
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool's geography lens carried the latitude with a negative sign, which would have put the landing in the South Atlantic, and the afterlife lens carried it correctly
stops.campa: After nearly three months at sea the Centaur lands him at Plymouth, and the British authorities receive the deposed governor of Buenos Aires with a salute of twenty-one guns, the honors of a head of state. Nobody in the country he has arrived in knows what he was; the newspapers call him General Rosas, dictator of the Argentine Confederation, and lose interest inside a fortnight. He is fifty-nine in a month. He goes inland from the quay, and he never sees the Río de la Plata again.
suggested_refs: The Plymouth landing of 26 April 1852 and the British Admiralty's reception orders

stops.name: Swaythling, the rented farm
stops.date_confidence: year only: the tenancy is dated to 1852 without a month, necessarily after the 26 April landing; the geography and afterlife lenses give slightly different coordinates for Swaythling and the afterlife pin is used
stops.campa: He rents a farm at Swaythling outside Southampton and works it: cattle again, on a Hampshire holding instead of a province the size of France. He keeps a housekeeper and hires local laborers, whom he pays above the going rate. Money is short, since the Argentine government has confiscated everything he owned and what comes from home arrives irregularly. He rises before light, rides, farms, and writes letters to Argentina that go on being political long after there is any politics left in them for him.
stops.quote: I now consider myself happy on this farm, living in modest circumstances as you see.
stops.quote_source: Rosas in exile at Swaythling, quoted in en.wikipedia.org, 'Juan Manuel de Rosas'
suggested_refs: The Swaythling farm tenancy and Rosas's exile correspondence, 1852-1877

stops.name: Southampton, the marriage of Manuelita
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the coordinate is approximate to central Southampton because the Spanish article does not identify the church
stops.campa: Manuela Rosas marries Máximo Terrero in a Catholic church in Southampton, six months into the exile. She had kept her father's house and his correspondence since she was twenty-one, received the diplomatic corps for him, and been the one door through which anyone reached him. The marriage is the first thing she does for herself. Terrero is the son of her father's oldest business partner. She is thirty-five, she never returns to Argentina, and her father does not ask her to stay unmarried a day longer.
suggested_refs: The Southampton parish register of the Rosas-Terrero marriage, 22 October 1852

stops.name: Southampton, death at eighty-three
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool's geography lens gave his age as eighty-four and claimed the sources disagreed, which they do not, both giving eighty-three
stops.campa: He walks out in cold weather, takes pneumonia and dies at eighty-three, sixteen days short of his eighty-fourth birthday, in the twenty-fifth year of an exile that no Argentine government ever offered to end. He is farming to the last season. Sarmiento, who wrote the book that fixed him as the monster of the century, has since been president of the republic and is alive in Buenos Aires. The funeral is private: the family, a priest, a few friends, and no delegation from the country he governed or from the one that condemned him.
suggested_refs: The death certificate and private funeral of March 1877 at Southampton

stops.name: Southampton Old Cemetery, the grave in foreign ground
stops.date_confidence: month only: the sources give March 1877 for the funeral and burial without a day, so the entry defaults to the first of the month; the two lenses of the pool also give slightly different coordinates for the cemetery
stops.campa: They bury him in the municipal cemetery of Southampton, in the ground of a country he had once fought a naval war against, among the graves of shipowners and merchant captains. The stone carries his name and his years. For a hundred and twelve years this is where he stays, and the Argentines who cross to England to argue that he was right make the trip out to the cemetery to stand at it, while the government at home keeps his name off the streets and out of the schoolbooks.
suggested_refs: The Rosas plot in Southampton Old Cemetery, occupied 1877 to 1989

segments.name: The Sentence and the Return of the Bones

stops.name: Buenos Aires, condemned in absentia
stops.date_confidence: year only: the pool dates the confiscation and the sentence to 1852 without a month, so the entry defaults to 1 January although both necessarily follow the February defeat
stops.campa: The government that replaces him confiscates everything he owns, tries him in absentia, condemns him to death and declares him a traitor to the country. The sentence can never be carried out and is not meant to be; it is a statement about which past the new republic intends to have. The caserón at Palermo passes to the state. His estancias and his houses are sold or granted away, and for the rest of the century to be a rosista in Buenos Aires is to stand outside the political nation altogether.
suggested_refs: The 1852 acts of confiscation and the sentence of death in absentia

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the revisionist reversal
stops.date_confidence: span, defaulted to the first year: the pool dates the counter-history from the 1880s and its organized form to the nacionalismo of the 1920s and 1930s, with no single founding date
stops.campa: From the 1880s a counter-history begins to be written, and by the 1920s and 1930s the revisionismo histórico of the Argentine nationalists has completed the reversal: not a tyrant but the defender of sovereignty, the man who kept the rivers shut against the fleets of Europe and was brought down for it by the port, the foreigners and the exiles who then wrote the textbooks. The academic historians do not accept it. The quarrel outlives everyone with a stake in the events and is still a fault line of Argentine historiography.
stops.quote: Rosas is a negative memory in Argentina. He left behind him the black legend of Argentine history, a legend which Argentines in general wish to forget.
stops.quote_source: William Dusenberry (1961), quoted in en.wikipedia.org, 'Juan Manuel de Rosas'. The original prints a dash where this rendering has a comma
suggested_refs: The Instituto de Investigaciones Históricas Juan Manuel de Rosas and the revisionist literature of the 1930s
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Juan Manuel de Rosas', citing William Dusenberry (1961)

stops.name: London, the death of Manuelita
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Manuela Rosas de Terrero dies in London at eighty-one, forty-six years after she went aboard the Centaur, having never gone back. She had outlived the government her father ran and most of the generation that hated it. In Buenos Aires, five months after her death, the last standing walls of the caserón at Palermo will be blown up. The exile that began as a passage under a foreign flag closes as an English household with an Argentine name, and no member of it is buried in the Río de la Plata.
suggested_refs: Manuela Rosas de Terrero's London years and the family papers she kept

stops.name: Parque Tres de Febrero, the caserón dynamited
stops.date_confidence: attested to the night of 2 to 3 February 1899; the pool's geography lens wrongly stated the caserón had been demolished after Caseros in 1852
stops.campa: The caserón of San Benito has stood forty-seven years past its owner's fall when the intendente Adolfo Bullrich has it dynamited in the night of the second of February 1899, timed so that nothing of it is standing at dawn on the anniversary of Caseros. The park laid over the ground is Sarmiento's work, and Sarmiento's own monument is inaugurated on it on 25 May 1900. A century after that, on the site of the caserón's Maestranza building, the state raises a monument to Rosas a few hundred metres from where his house came down.
suggested_refs: The Maestranza site in Parque Tres de Febrero, ground of both the caserón and the later Rosas monument

stops.name: Vuelta de Obligado, the Day of Sovereignty
stops.date_confidence: year only: the declaration of 20 November as the Day of Sovereignty is dated 1974 and the national holiday 2010, neither with a day in the pool
stops.campa: At the bend of the Paraná where the chains were stretched, the state builds a monument to the battle, and a sculpture bearing Rosas's image stands in it. The twentieth of November is declared the Day of Sovereignty in 1974 and made a national holiday in 2010, and schoolchildren are taught the forcing of the river as the day the country said no to two empires at once. The battle was lost. The doctrine that a river belongs to the country whose banks it runs between was not, and no Argentine government has disowned it.
suggested_refs: The monument at the Vuelta de Obligado and the 1974 and 2010 decrees on the Día de la Soberanía

stops.name: La Recoleta, the bones brought home
stops.date_confidence: attested by the biography article; the Recoleta article gives only the year, and the two lenses of the pool differ in the fourth decimal of the longitude
stops.campa: A hundred and twelve years after his death the remains come home. They are lifted out of Southampton Old Cemetery and brought to Buenos Aires, and on 30 September 1989 the government of Carlos Menem lays them in the family vault at the Recoleta, a short walk from where Encarnación has lain since 1838. The president calls it a reconciliation between unitarios and federales, a hundred and thirty-seven years after Caseros. The argument over whether it should have happened at all resumes the following morning.
suggested_refs: The Ortiz de Rozas vault at the Cementerio de la Recoleta and the repatriation ceremony of 30 September 1989
